### I. The Principle of the Plumb Line

The brass transit smelled of machine oil and cold river silt, an odor that belonged to another century, though the leather of its carrying case was fresh enough to squeak against Julian’s shoulder as he climbed. 

He had walked since dawn along the contour lines of a map that had ceased to be accurate before his father was born. The valley below him was shaped like a dry leaf: narrow at the stem where the creek had once tumbled through a throat of slate, broad and pale in the middle where the orchards had withered into gray brush, and frayed at the northern lip where the gravel road gave up its gravel to the sand.

Julian worked for the Department of Residual Demarcation. It was an agency whose funding had been forgotten by three successive administrative reorganizations, tucked away beneath the Department of Canals and Drainage in an obscure wing of the capital’s gray stone archive. His salary arrived quarterly in the form of a paper warrant stamped with a seal depicting a surveyor’s wheel entwined with wheat—an emblem from an agricultural era that no living clerk could remember. Julian cashed these warrants at a discount in tavern backrooms and bought flour, lard, salt, cartridges for his carbine, and the pale blue linen-backed paper upon which he drew his plates.

His assignment, broadly stated, was to ascertain what remained when a place had concluded.

Every landscape, Julian’s former superior had once told him over a plate of stewed tripe in a damp cellar near the railyards, was an argument between human intention and the stubborn indifference of geology. Human intention had the advantage of speed, but geology had the leisure of eternity. In the end, the stones always won, but Julian’s duty was not to celebrate the stone; it was to record the terms of surrender.

He set the three legs of his cedar tripod into the caliche crust at the crest of the ridge. The wind here was steady, coming off the alkaline flats with the faint, sharp smell of dried brine and sage. He leveled the leveling screws with careful quarter-turns of his thumb and forefinger, watching the green bubble drift into its brass cage like a captured eye. When it rested dead center between the two engraved black hairlines, he bent his neck to the eyepiece.

Through the optics, inverted and swimming in amber light, the town appeared.

It was called Black Kettle on the 1884 surveys, though earlier German maps had marked it as *Kesselsbrunn*, and the railroad circulars of 1902 had briefly, hopefully, baptized it *New Palmyra*. None of these names had taken root deeply enough to outlive the water table. When the artesian head dropped below two hundred feet in the summer of the drought, the cottonwood leaves had curled like charred paper, and within five seasons the houses had begun to lose their windowpanes to the crows and the hail.

Through the crosshairs, Julian picked out the geometry of the loss. 

There were eleven structures still standing with four walls, eight with three, and nineteen that had fallen into the shape of sunken ships—hulls of weathered lath and cedar shingles resting in troughs of their own cellar holes. At the end of what had been Commercial Street stood the false-fronted facade of the general store, its painted sign stripped of its vowels by thirty years of scouring dust: *M R C A N T I L E*.

A single curl of pale smoke was rising from the stovepipe of the former livery stable.

Julian did not look at the smoke for long. He uncapped his brass inkhorn, hooked it to his waistcoat button, and opened the black morocco-bound field book. With a bone-handled ruling pen, he struck his baseline across the grid.

***

### II. The Inhabitant of the Margin

The horse was dead; the stable smelled only of straw that had turned to tinder and the dry droppings of mice.

In the harness room, where harness oil had once kept the leather supple against the sweat of draught teams, a woman sat on an upturned nail keg peeling an onion with a paring knife whose blade had been ground down to the width of a willow leaf. She wore a coat made from three different army blankets, sewn together with thick, waxed twine, the stitches coarse as teeth. Her hair was not gray so much as faded, the color of wet wood that has dried in the sun until its grain shows through.

She did not look up when Julian’s shadow crossed the threshold, though she laid the knife across her knee.

"The wind’s from the east," she said. Her voice had the dry, rustling friction of maize husks. "You’ve brought dust on your trousers."

"The road is loose above the culvert," Julian said. He took off his hat and held it against his ribs. "The Ministry sends its regards."

"The Ministry doesn't know where this valley is," she said. She dropped an onion skin into a tin basin between her feet. The skin was paper-dry and made a sharp, papery click. "The Ministry thinks this is sheep commons. It was sheep commons under the old king, before the canal company took the liens."

"The liens were voided forty years ago," Julian said gently.

"Then the sheep should come back," she said. "They had better manners than the surveyors."

Her name was Martha, though she had also answered to Mrs. Gedge, though whether Gedge was a husband, a father, or a peddler who had died on her floor was something she refused to clarify. She had lived in Black Kettle through three distinct cycles of departure: first the wheat farmers who had sold their teams to buy rail tickets to the coast; then the silver prospectors who had spent two frantic summers digging trenches into the red basalt of the ridge before finding only pyrites and gypsum; and finally the three brothers who had tried to pasture goats on the greasewood flats until the water tasted too much of alum for the kids to thrive.

"Are you the only one left on the roll?" Julian asked. He had brought out his register—the long, narrow folio bound in blue marbled board.

"There is no roll," Martha said. "The preacher took the register with him when he went north. He said the names belonged to God, but he took them in his carpetbag just the same. He thought there was coal under the cemetery. He had an idea that if he kept the book, he kept the deeds to the graves."

"And did he?"

"The cemetery went down the wash in the flood of twenty-six," she said. She sliced through the heart of the onion; a small, sharp bead of juice showed on the steel. "The water came out of the canyon like a gray wall. The markers were only cedar shingles, mostly. They floated down toward the sinks like little boats. I found one three miles south, stuck in a chokecherry bush. It said *Hester, Aged Two Years*. I used it for kindling when the frost came that November. A two-year-old wouldn't hold a grudge against a fire."

Julian dipped his pen into the inkhorn. The ink was iron-gall, dark purple when wet, drying to the color of dried liver.

"I need to record the perimeter," he said. "The Ministry requires an accurate return on the decay of the civic boundary."

Martha looked at him then. Her eyes were small, wet, and remarkably clear, like two pebbles under an inch of creek water.

"You have very fine hands for an undertaker," she said.

"I am an engineer," Julian replied, though he felt the truth of her word settle somewhere behind his collarbone like a cold draft.

"An engineer builds things that stand up," she said, rising with the basin. "You’re just measuring how fast they fall down so somebody in an office can write a number in a column and go home to his tea. Come along then. If you’re going to walk the line, you might as well carry the bucket."

***

### III. The Taxonomy of the Unused

They walked the perimeter of the former townsite through the middle hours of the afternoon, while the sun hung over the ridge like a flat, white wafer.

Julian carried the brass surveyor’s chain—sixty-six feet of links, worn smooth where the iron rings rubbed against one another, chiming with a muffled, metallic rattle at every step. Martha walked ahead of him with an ash stick, pointing out what had vanished with the authority of an empress displaying her gardens.

"Here was the apothecary," she said, stopping before an oblong depression where wild mustard grew twice as tall as on the open flat. "He had four jars of blue water in his window. When the sun struck them in the morning, they threw spots of blue light across the dirt like robins' eggs. He had a machine with two brass rollers that pressed pills out of paste. It went *clack-whir, clack-whir*. When his wife died of the quinsy, he threw the machine into the well and walked out toward the gap with a bundle under his arm. He didn't even take his boots; he wore his slippers with the carpet-work on the toes."

Julian dropped an iron pin into the earth to mark the chain-end. "Did anyone drag the well?"

"What for? Nobody wanted pills. They wanted flour and they wanted the wind to stop. You can’t dredge flour out of forty feet of sour water."

They proceeded south by twenty degrees east. The town had been platted on the Jeffersonian grid, that great democratic net cast over the continent’s irregularities, but here the grid had frayed against the topography. A dry wash had cut through Tenth Street, carrying away three platted blocks that had never contained anything more substantial than surveyors' stakes and prairie dog burrows.

Julian knelt to note the bearing. The field book was filling with his precise, spider-web entries:

> *Sta. IV to Sta. V: 4 chains, 12 links. Azimuth 198°30'.*
> *Soil: Calcareous loam, alkaline encrustation to depth of 2 inches.*
> *Vegetation: Atriplex canescens, Gutierrezia sarothrae.*
> *Structural remains: One stone hearth (sandstone, dry-laid, 4' x 3'), lintel fractured by heat. One cedar splay, notched for rafters, rotted at base.*
> *Residual population: 1 female, age indeterminate.*

"What do you write about me?" Martha asked, leaning over his shoulder. Her coat smelled of old grease, chicory, and the cold wool of long-dead sheep.

"I write that you are here," Julian said.

"That's not enough," she said. "You should write that I have nine jars of pickled gooseberries left in the cellar under the blacksmith’s shop, and that four of them have gone cloudy. You should write that the chimney swallows have stopped building in the church flue because the soot has turned into poison from the smelter smoke thirty miles away. You should write that the wind makes the sound of a fiddle string through the telegraph wire when it comes from the north, but when it comes from the south it sounds like a dog whining under a porch."

Julian held his pen suspended above the paper. The breeze dried the ink on the nib before he could touch it to the sheet.

"The Department does not have a column for the sound of the wire," he said.

"Then your book is only half-full," she said, "and you ought to ask for half-wages."

She turned and poked her stick into a pile of rusted tins. The labels had disappeared decades ago, but the metal had dissolved into lacy, red-brown skeletons that collapsed into powder at the tap of her ash pole.

"People leave the strangest things when they go," she remarked, almost conversationally. "They’ll leave an iron bedstead that cost twelve dollars from the catalog, but they’ll take a cracked teacup that isn't worth a copper penny because their grandmother carried it across the salt flats in her apron. They’ll take an old clock that doesn't keep time and leave three barrels of salt pork behind because the pork is heavy and the clock has a picture of a church painted on the glass. When the Miller family left, they took their birdcage, but they let the canary go. It sat on the well-pulley for three days, yellow as a lemon, looking at the sagebrush. It didn't know what to do with all that sky. A hawk took it on the fourth morning. It didn't even drop a feather."

Julian looked up toward the ridge where his tripod stood silhouetted against the blinding zinc of the sky. From this distance, the instrument looked like an insect that had settled on the edge of the world to watch the valley drain of its substance.

"Why did you stay, Martha?"

She stopped her poking. Her face was turned away from him, toward the gap where the road dissolved into the gray expanse of the lower basin.

"Someone has to remember where the doors were," she said. "If nobody remembers where the doors were, then people will think this was always just stones and dust. It wasn't just stones and dust. We had a choir. We had twenty-two people who could sing *The Rose of Sharon* without the organ, and two of them were tenors who could hit the high G without their voices cracking. You can't let a valley forget that it once had two good tenors. It isn't fair to the valley."

***

### IV. The Mechanics of Dissolution

In the evening, they sat in the harness room by the light of a lard-lamp that Martha had improvised from a cracked saucer and a strip of cotton shirting.

The flame was small, smokeless, and cast a greasy yellow circle across the rough table. Julian had spread his working map over the boards, weighting its corners with four iron square-cut nails he had pulled from the livery jamb.

"This is the fifth town I’ve closed this year," Julian said. His fingers were stiff with the evening cold that dropped out of the mountains the moment the sun cleared the rim. "In May, it was a landing on the river called Saint-Pierre-des-Oies. The river changed its course during the spring rise; it cut a new channel through the willow bottoms four miles west. The steamboats stopped whistling. By the time I arrived, the wharf had slid into the mud and the schoolteacher had taken down the school bell and buried it in his garden so the bailiff couldn't take it for the school district’s debts."

"Did you dig it up?" Martha asked. She was mending an old wool sock with a needle made from an umbrella rib.

"No," Julian said. "I recorded its mass and approximate depth from the teacher's affidavit, and I marked the site as *Unimproved Commons with Subsurface Iron.*"

"You’re a cold creature, Julian."

"The state cannot be sentimental, Martha. If the state were sentimental, it would have to pay for the funerals of all its roads."

"And doesn't it?"

"It lets them grass over," he said. "A road that isn't traveled is simply dirt that has been compressed for a little while. The grass understands that better than the men who laid the macadam."

He took his bone-handled compass and began to describe an arc from the point marked *Public Well (Contaminated)*. The iron leg of the instrument dug into the blue paper with a faint tearing sound.

"Tell me about the train," he said.

Martha dropped her hands into her lap. The sock was gray, worn through at the heel until it looked like a spider’s web.

"It only came three times a week," she said. "The engine was small—a wood-burner with a funnel like an acorn. It had an engineer named Mr. Clough who had lost three fingers on his left hand in the roundhouse at the junction. When he pulled the whistle cord, he used his right elbow. It sounded like an old sheep bleating in a rain barrel."

She looked at the lard-lamp, her eyes narrowing as if she could see the iron rails running through the wick.

"The day they took the rails up," she whispered, "that was worse than the day the water failed. When the water failed, we thought we could dig deeper. Men spent their Sundays with augers and dynamite, coming up from the holes with red mud in their ears and eyes, swearing that they’d smelled sweet water just five feet below where the drill broke. But when the rail-gang came with their crowbars and their flatcars, there was no arguing with them. They were Irishmen and Swedes who didn't care about Black Kettle. They pulled up the spikes with long pinch-bars that went *thunk-creak*. Every time a spike came out of a tie, it sounded like a tooth being pulled from an old man's jaw."

"They needed the iron for the coal branch," Julian said.

"They threw the ties into piles and burned them," she continued, ignoring him. "The creosote smelled like roasted nuts. We stood on the bank—thirty of us, all that was left—and watched them burn fifteen miles of larch ties. The fire ran along the right-of-way like a red snake. It burned for four nights. You could read a newspaper on your porch at midnight by the light of those ties. When they were done, there was just a black strip through the sage, like someone had drawn a line with a piece of charcoal across the valley."

"And then?"

"And then the morning came," she said, "and there was nothing to listen for."

Julian looked down at his map. In the space between the western ridge and the salt wash, where the black hatch-marks of the grade were drawn, he wrote in small, immaculate script: *Right-of-way abandoned 1911. Ballast reclaimed by natural agency.*

"You have very neat letters," she said. "They look like little iron fences."

"They are meant to be permanent," he said.

"Nothing is permanent that's written in grease and gall," said Martha. "My mother had a Bible with all our births in it. She kept it in the bottom of the meal chest. When the roof leaked while we were down with the ague, the water got into the meal and made a paste of it. The paste dried like stone around the book. When we chopped it out with a hatchet, the pages were all stuck together like salt cod. You couldn't tell who had been born in seventy-two and who had died in eighty-six. We were all just one big cake of white dough."

She stood up and blew through her teeth. The flame of the lard-lamp guttered, rose high and thin, then settled into a smoky bead.

"There's a cot in the harness room," she said. "The canvas is whole, though the ticks have got into the straw. If you sleep with your boots on, they won't bite your ankles."

"Thank you, Martha."

"Don't thank me. You’re going to write down tomorrow that I'm crazy, and next year they'll send two men with a spring-wagon and an order from the county judge to take me down to the asylum at the river."

Julian looked at her steadily. "There is no county judge," he said. "The county was disincorporated in the autumn session of the legislature. You belong to no jurisdiction at all."

She paused by the door, the ash stick tucked beneath her arm like an officer's baton.

"Then I am the queen of it," she said.

***

### V. The Field of Triangulation

Julian did not sleep on the canvas cot.

When the house had gone completely silent—a silence so dense that he could hear the sand grains shifting against the foundation stones like salt falling through an hourglass—he took his lantern and his transit back up the trail to the ridge.

The air at midnight was cold enough to make his nostrils stick together. The sky was not black; it was a deep, vitrified indigo, so clear that the stars did not appear to be set into a dome, but hung at terrifying, disparate depths, some near and amber-colored, others infinitely small and blue, receding into the emptiness like lanterns carried by people walking away across an endless meadow.

He leveled the transit by starlight.

His eyes had adapted to the dark, and the brass parts had taken on the pale, ghostly sheen of wet bone. He pointed the objective toward the northern horizon, searching for the benchmark he had established three days ago on the limestone shoulder of Mount Disappointment.

It was a small cairn of white rocks, five feet high, with an iron rod set in its apex. He found it by the faint silhouette it cast against the lower stars: a sharp, deliberate interruption of the mountain’s ragged spine.

He checked his vernier: zero degrees, zero minutes, zero seconds.

Then he turned the horizontal plate south, toward the valley of the sinks.

In the circle of his lens, thirty miles away across the black floor of the desert, a small yellow point was burning.

It was not a star. It was too low, resting precisely on the line where the earth met the sky. It was too red, too unsteady, trembling through the heat radiation that the alkaline flats were still breathing into the cold upper air.

He knew what it was. It was the smelting works at Oreana—the sixty-foot stacks where they roasted the lead-silver concentrate from the deep shafts. They had been burning there day and night for forty years. Men worked twelve-hour shifts in the fumes with sponges tied over their mouths, their gums blue with lead-palsy, their wheelbarrows creaking under the weight of the dross. The smoke from those stacks was what had killed Martha’s swallows; the silver that came from those furnaces was what had paid for the surveyors who had drawn the first grid through this basin.

He read the angle off the plate: 174° 16' 45".

He wrote it down in the field book by the red light of a sulfur match. The match flared, hissed, smelled of the pit, and died, leaving its blue after-image floating between Julian’s eye and the paper.

He looked down into the hollow where Black Kettle lay.

There was no light there at all. Not even the lantern from the stable. The stable was only a square shadow slightly darker than the gray of the brush. It was incredible to think that within that dark square, a woman was breathing, her lungs expanding and contracting with air that had traveled five thousand miles across the Pacific Ocean to cross an empty coast, an empty mountain range, and an empty flat, only to be drawn into the throat of an old woman who remembered the names of two tenors.

Julian leaned his forehead against the cold brass of the telescope barrel.

His work was an absurdity, and he knew it. You cannot measure an absence. You can only measure the things that border it—the stone, the fence line, the dry ditch, the angle between a mountain named after a failure and a smelter named after an ore. The town itself was not in the book; the book was only a frame around a hole in the world.

He thought of his office in the capital. The rows of green-painted shelves stretching down long, vaulted corridors where gas jets hissed in their wire cages. The thousands of rolls of linen paper, tied with red tape, upon which were recorded the names of villages that had drowned in reservoirs, towns that had burned to the rock in the forest fires of eighty-nine, settlements that had simply faded out of existence because the road had turned four miles to the left to follow a butter-factory rather than a dry creek.

Those maps were not preserved so that anyone could find those places again. They were preserved so that the clerks could prove that the state had been there first. They were the receipt the empire kept against the day when the land would demand its money back.

He raised his head.

A great meteor fell across the east, dropping from the constellation of the Plow toward the gray ridges like a white-hot nail dropped into water. For half a second, the valley returned to sight: the bleached roofs of the eleven houses, the white track of the dry road, the pale ribs of the livery stable, and the immense, white expanse of the salt flat beyond, shining like a sheet of ice on an inland sea that had vanished before the first lizard had learned to crawl.

Then the darkness closed behind it, heavier than before.

Julian uncapped his pen once more. He did not light another match. He knew the format by heart; his hand had made the entry two hundred times in sixty different valleys:

> *General Remarks: The location presents no further administrative utility. The infrastructure has returned to the soil. The water is insufficient for mechanical or pastoral use. The remaining inhabitant is non-viable. The survey is complete.*

He hesitated. The wind came up from the sinks, cold and sharp, smelling of ancient salt and the bitter grease of greasewood.

He held the nib against the bottom of the page for a long time, until the ink began to spread into the blue fibers, forming a small, irregular blot like an insect that had died while trying to cross the linen.

Then, beneath the signature of the surveyor, he wrote:

> *The tenors were two in number. The high G was reached without cracking.*

He closed the book. He strapped the brass transit into its leather case, buckled the straps until they bit into the oil-dark hide, and shouldered the tripod.

The eastern sky was beginning to turn the color of wet tin. He did not go back down to the harness room to say goodbye to Martha; he knew she would be awake, and he knew that she would be peeling her onion or scraping her turnip, and he did not want to see the small, white knife moving in her hand.

He turned his back on the town and began the long walk south along the ridge, following the dry contour lines toward the railline forty miles away, where the morning train would be whistling for a station that still had an agent, a ledger, and a clock with three brass weights that dropped through the dark to measure the length of the hours.

He didn't even take his boots; he wore his slippers with the carpet-work on the toes."

Julian dropped an iron pin into the earth to mark the chain-end. "Did anyone drag the well?"

"What for? Nobody wanted pills. They wanted flour and they wanted the wind to stop. You can’t dredge flour out of forty feet of sour water."

They proceeded south by twenty degrees east. The town had been platted on the Jeffersonian grid, that great democratic net cast over the continent’s irregularities, but here the grid had frayed against the topography. A dry wash had cut through Tenth Street, carrying away three platted blocks that had never contained anything more substantial than surveyors' stakes and prairie dog burrows.

Julian knelt to note the bearing. The field book was filling with his precise, spider-web entries:

> *Sta. IV to Sta. V: 4 chains, 12 links. Azimuth 198°30'.*
> *Soil: Calcareous loam, alkaline encrustation to depth of 2 inches.*
> *Vegetation: Atriplex canescens, Gutierrezia sarothrae.*
> *Structural remains: One stone hearth (sandstone, dry-laid, 4' x 3'), lintel fractured by heat. One cedar splay, notched for rafters, rotted at base.*
> *Residual population: 1 female, age indeterminate.*

"What do you write about me?" Martha asked, leaning over his shoulder. Her coat smelled of old grease, chicory, and the cold wool of long-dead sheep.

"I write that you are here," Julian said.

"That's not enough," she said. "You should write that I have nine jars of pickled gooseberries left in the cellar under the blacksmith’s shop, and that four of them have gone cloudy. You should write that the chimney swallows have stopped building in the church flue because the soot has turned into poison from the smelter smoke thirty miles away. You should write that the wind makes the sound of a fiddle string through the telegraph wire when it comes from the north, but when it comes from the south it sounds like a dog whining under a porch."

Julian held his pen suspended above the paper. The breeze dried the ink on the nib before he could touch it to the sheet.

"The Department does not have a column for the sound of the wire," he said.

"Then your book is only half-full," she said, "and you ought to ask for half-wages."

She turned and poked her stick into a pile of rusted tins. The labels had disappeared decades ago, but the metal had dissolved into lacy, red-brown skeletons that collapsed into powder at the tap of her ash pole.

"People leave the strangest things when they go," she remarked, almost conversationally. "They’ll leave an iron bedstead that cost twelve dollars from the catalog, but they’ll take a cracked teacup that isn't worth a copper penny because their grandmother carried it across the salt flats in her apron. They’ll take an old clock that doesn't keep time and leave three barrels of salt pork behind because the pork is heavy and the clock has a picture of a church painted on the glass. When the Miller family left, they took their birdcage, but they let the canary go. It sat on the well-pulley for three days, yellow as a lemon, looking at the sagebrush. It didn't know what to do with all that sky. A hawk took it on the fourth morning. It didn't even drop a feather."

Julian looked up toward the ridge where his tripod stood silhouetted against the blinding zinc of the sky. From this distance, the instrument looked like an insect that had settled on the edge of the world to watch the valley drain of its substance.

"Why did you stay, Martha?"

She stopped her poking. Her face was turned away from him, toward the gap where the road dissolved into the gray expanse of the lower basin.

"Someone has to remember where the doors were," she said. "If nobody remembers where the doors were, then people will think this was always just stones and dust. It wasn't just stones and dust. We had a choir. We had twenty-two people who could sing *The Rose of Sharon* without the organ, and two of them were tenors who could hit the high G without their voices cracking. You can't let a valley forget that it once had two good tenors. It isn't fair to the valley."

***

### IV. The Mechanics of Dissolution

In the evening, they sat in the harness room by the light of a lard-lamp that Martha had improvised from a cracked saucer and a strip of cotton shirting.

The flame was small, smokeless, and cast a greasy yellow circle across the rough table. Julian had spread his working map over the boards, weighting its corners with four iron square-cut nails he had pulled from the livery jamb.

"This is the fifth town I’ve closed this year," Julian said. His fingers were stiff with the evening cold that dropped out of the mountains the moment the sun cleared the rim. "In May, it was a landing on the river called Saint-Pierre-des-Oies. The river changed its course during the spring rise; it cut a new channel through the willow bottoms four miles west. The steamboats stopped whistling. By the time I arrived, the wharf had slid into the mud and the schoolteacher had taken down the school bell and buried it in his garden so the bailiff couldn't take it for the school district’s debts."

"Did you dig it up?" Martha asked. She was mending an old wool sock with a needle made from an umbrella rib.

"No," Julian said. "I recorded its mass and approximate depth from the teacher's affidavit, and I marked the site as *Unimproved Commons with Subsurface Iron.*"

"You’re a cold creature, Julian."

"The state cannot be sentimental, Martha. If the state were sentimental, it would have to pay for the funerals of all its roads."

"And doesn't it?"

"It lets them grass over," he said. "A road that isn't traveled is simply dirt that has been compressed for a little while. The grass understands that better than the men who laid the macadam."

He took his bone-handled compass and began to describe an arc from the point marked *Public Well (Contaminated)*. The iron leg of the instrument dug into the blue paper with a faint tearing sound.

"Tell me about the train," he said.

Martha dropped her hands into her lap. The sock was gray, worn through at the heel until it looked like a spider’s web.

"It only came three times a week," she said. "The engine was small—a wood-burner with a funnel like an acorn. It had an engineer named Mr. Clough who had lost three fingers on his left hand in the roundhouse at the junction. When he pulled the whistle cord, he used his right elbow. It sounded like an old sheep bleating in a rain barrel."

She looked at the lard-lamp, her eyes narrowing as if she could see the iron rails running through the wick.

"The day they took the rails up," she whispered, "that was worse than the day the water failed. When the water failed, we thought we could dig deeper. Men spent their Sundays with augers and dynamite, coming up from the holes with red mud in their ears and eyes, swearing that they’d smelled sweet water just five feet below where the drill broke. But when the rail-gang came with their crowbars and their flatcars, there was no arguing with them. They were Irishmen and Swedes who didn't care about Black Kettle. They pulled up the spikes with long pinch-bars that went *thunk-creak*. Every time a spike came out of a tie, it sounded like a tooth being pulled from an old man's jaw."

"They needed the iron for the coal branch," Julian said.

"They threw the ties into piles and burned them," she continued, ignoring him. "The creosote smelled like roasted nuts. We stood on the bank—thirty of us, all that was left—and watched them burn fifteen miles of larch ties. The fire ran along the right-of-way like a red snake. It burned for four nights. You could read a newspaper on your porch at midnight by the light of those ties. When they were done, there was just a black strip through the sage, like someone had drawn a line with a piece of charcoal across the valley."

"And then?"

"And then the morning came," she said, "and there was nothing to listen for."

Julian looked down at his map. In the space between the western ridge and the salt wash, where the black hatch-marks of the grade were drawn, he wrote in small, immaculate script: *Right-of-way abandoned 1911. Ballast reclaimed by natural agency.*

"You have very neat letters," she said. "They look like little iron fences."

"They are meant to be permanent," he said.

"Nothing is permanent that's written in grease and gall," said Martha. "My mother had a Bible with all our births in it. She kept it in the bottom of the meal chest. When the roof leaked while we were down with the ague, the water got into the meal and made a paste of it. The paste dried like stone around the book. When we chopped it out with a hatchet, the pages were all stuck together like salt cod. You couldn't tell who had been born in seventy-two and who had died in eighty-six. We were all just one big cake of white dough."

She stood up and blew through her teeth. The flame of the lard-lamp guttered, rose high and thin, then settled into a smoky bead.

"There's a cot in the harness room," she said. "The canvas is whole, though the ticks have got into the straw. If you sleep with your boots on, they won't bite your ankles."

"Thank you, Martha."

"Don't thank me. You’re going to write down tomorrow that I'm crazy, and next year they'll send two men with a spring-wagon and an order from the county judge to take me down to the asylum at the river."

Julian looked at her steadily. "There is no county judge," he said. "The county was disincorporated in the autumn session of the legislature. You belong to no jurisdiction at all."

She paused by the door, the ash stick tucked beneath her arm like an officer's baton.

"Then I am the queen of it," she said.

***

### V. The Field of Triangulation

Julian did not sleep on the canvas cot.

When the house had gone completely silent—a silence so dense that he could hear the sand grains shifting against the foundation stones like salt falling through an hourglass—he took his lantern and his transit back up the trail to the ridge.

The air at midnight was cold enough to make his nostrils stick together. The sky was not black; it was a deep, vitrified indigo, so clear that the stars did not appear to be set into a dome, but hung at terrifying, disparate depths, some near and amber-colored, others infinitely small and blue, receding into the emptiness like lanterns carried by people walking away across an endless meadow.

He leveled the transit by starlight.

His eyes had adapted to the dark, and the brass parts had taken on the pale, ghostly sheen of wet bone. He pointed the objective toward the northern horizon, searching for the benchmark he had established three days ago on the limestone shoulder of Mount Disappointment.

It was a small cairn of white rocks, five feet high, with an iron rod set in its apex. He found it by the faint silhouette it cast against the lower stars: a sharp, deliberate interruption of the mountain’s ragged spine.

He checked his vernier: zero degrees, zero minutes, zero seconds.

Then he turned the horizontal plate south, toward the valley of the sinks.

In the circle of his lens, thirty miles away across the black floor of the desert, a small yellow point was burning.

It was not a star. It was too low, resting precisely on the line where the earth met the sky. It was too red, too unsteady, trembling through the heat radiation that the alkaline flats were still breathing into the cold upper air.

He knew what it was. It was the smelting works at Oreana—the sixty-foot stacks where they roasted the lead-silver concentrate from the deep shafts. They had been burning there day and night for forty years. Men worked twelve-hour shifts in the fumes with sponges tied over their mouths, their gums blue with lead-palsy, their wheelbarrows creaking under the weight of the dross. The smoke from those stacks was what had killed Martha’s swallows; the silver that came from those furnaces was what had paid for the surveyors who had drawn the first grid through this basin.

He read the angle off the plate: 174° 16' 45".

He wrote it down in the field book by the red light of a sulfur match. The match flared, hissed, smelled of the pit, and died, leaving its blue after-image floating between Julian’s eye and the paper.

He looked down into the hollow where Black Kettle lay.

There was no light there at all. Not even the lantern from the stable. The stable was only a square shadow slightly darker than the gray of the brush. It was incredible to think that within that dark square, a woman was breathing, her lungs expanding and contracting with air that had traveled five thousand miles across the Pacific Ocean to cross an empty coast, an empty mountain range, and an empty flat, only to be drawn into the throat of an old woman who remembered the names of two tenors.

Julian leaned his forehead against the cold brass of the telescope barrel.

His work was an absurdity, and he knew it. You cannot measure an absence. You can only measure the things that border it—the stone, the fence line, the dry ditch, the angle between a mountain named after a failure and a smelter named after an ore. The town itself was not in the book; the book was only a frame around a hole in the world.

He thought of his office in the capital. The rows of green-painted shelves stretching down long, vaulted corridors where gas jets hissed in their wire cages. The thousands of rolls of linen paper, tied with red tape, upon which were recorded the names of villages that had drowned in reservoirs, towns that had burned to the rock in the forest fires of eighty-nine, settlements that had simply faded out of existence because the road had turned four miles to the left to follow a butter-factory rather than a dry creek.

Those maps were not preserved so that anyone could find those places again. They were preserved so that the clerks could prove that the state had been there first. They were the receipt the empire kept against the day when the land would demand its money back.

He raised his head.

A great meteor fell across the east, dropping from the constellation of the Plow toward the gray ridges like a white-hot nail dropped into water. For half a second, the valley returned to sight: the bleached roofs of the eleven houses, the white track of the dry road, the pale ribs of the livery stable, and the immense, white expanse of the salt flat beyond, shining like a sheet of ice on an inland sea that had vanished before the first lizard had learned to crawl.

Then the darkness closed behind it, heavier than before.

Julian uncapped his pen once more. He did not light another match. He knew the format by heart; his hand had made the entry two hundred times in sixty different valleys:

> *General Remarks: The location presents no further administrative utility. The infrastructure has returned to the soil. The water is insufficient for mechanical or pastoral use. The remaining inhabitant is non-viable. The survey is complete.*

He hesitated. The wind came up from the sinks, cold and sharp, smelling of ancient salt and the bitter grease of greasewood.

He held the nib against the bottom of the page for a long time, until the ink began to spread into the blue fibers, forming a small, irregular blot like an insect that had died while trying to cross the linen.

Then, beneath the signature of the surveyor, he wrote:

> *The tenors were two in number. The high G was reached without cracking.*

He closed the book. He strapped the brass transit into its leather case, buckled the straps until they bit into the oil-dark hide, and shouldered the tripod.

The eastern sky was beginning to turn the color of wet tin. He did not go back down to the harness room to say goodbye to Martha; he knew she would be awake, and he knew that she would be peeling her onion or scraping her turnip, and he did not want to see the small, white knife moving in her hand.

He turned his back on the town and began the long walk south along the ridge, following the dry contour lines toward the railline forty miles away, where the morning train would be whistling for a station that still had an agent, a ledger, and a clock with three brass weights that dropped through the dark to measure the length of the hours.
